LESSON 2 OF 106·Cyber Security Fundamentals

Cybersecurity vs Information Security

Cybersecurity and information security overlap but are not the same. Understand the difference, why regulators care, and how to classify what you are protecting.

Beginner12 min
Why this matters

Information security protects data wherever it lives. Cyber security is broader: it covers the technology, the networks and the services built on that data. The difference is scope, not intent.

What you'll learn

  • How it works
  • The background
  • Real-world examples
  • What to look for

How it works

  • Information security is about confidentiality, integrity and availability of information, regardless of the medium that holds it.
  • Cyber security adds the systems and supply chain: operating systems, networks, endpoints, identity providers, cloud platforms and third-party vendors.
  • A physical control such as a locked server room is an information-security measure expressed in a cyber environment.
  • Operational security covers the process side: who is allowed to change a system, how changes are approved, and how incidents are escalated.
  • The fields overlap heavily, and in most job descriptions the words are used interchangeably.

The background

  • The term information security grew out of document handling and records management, long before networked computing.
  • As systems became interconnected, the field split into computer security, network security and information security, because each layer needed different controls.
  • Cyber security emerged as an umbrella term in the 1990s as attacks shifted from isolated machines to connected enterprise networks.
  • Today the two words are largely interchangeable in job titles, and the distinction matters mainly when scoping a policy or a compliance regime.

Real-world examples

  • An ISO 27001 audit is an information-security exercise that necessarily covers the cyber systems holding that information.
  • A data-protection regulator focuses on personal data specifically, which is a subset of everything an organisation treats as information.
  • A lost company laptop is both a physical-security loss and an information-security loss, and the response depends on which data was on it.

What to look for

  • Ask which asset class is at stake: data, a running service, a device, or a person safety.
  • Check whether a control protects the information or merely the system that serves it.
  • Notice when a vendor promises a security product but never states which information it is meant to protect.

Practice / apply

Use a suitable learning environment and follow the resource's instructions. Test other people's systems only with permission.

Key takeaways

  • Write policies against the data and services you care about rather than against the tool you happen to own.
  • Map regulatory obligations to the specific information they cover.
  • Keep physical, operational and technical controls in one register so gaps between them are visible.
